title: Independent image tests find stronger texture signal but do not resolve greater concentration in public macaque V2
abstract: We tested whether a common response to higher-order texture structure can explain spectral compression in the Freeman/Ziemba Brain-Score public split. We used 102 V1 and 103 V2 neurons and 13 texture families with at least two naturalistic and two noise images. An exact cross-product estimator excludes same-image and same-trial terms. Generalizable texture-minus-noise energy was 0.01575 in V1 and 0.07449 in V2, in squared standardized counts per neuron. Common energy was 0.00653 and 0.02879. V2 retained larger total and common energy after each family omission. A trial-only common fraction rose from 0.121 to 0.241. Independent-image fractions were 0.414 and 0.386; their difference was unresolved because V1 energy was weak. Mixing textures and noise did not reveal steeper V2 response spectra. Thus stronger texture signal does not establish greater concentration in this split. The method separates fixed-image responses from texture signal that transfers across examples. Broad V2 texture preference is known prior work. Limits include few images, conditional neuron-and-family intervals, no animal-level replication, and no causal test of the mouse mechanism.

display.caption: Texture-minus-noise energy across independent images and trials. V2 has stronger total and common signal. Common fractions do not establish a concentration increase; the independent-image V1 ratio is unstable. Intervals resample neurons and families conditional on observed images.

citations.reason: Same public macaque assembly and spectral null motivate a contrast-specific test.
Mouse feature emergence and residual compression motivate the mechanism question.
Original recordings and established V2 texture preference.
Separate macaque recordings report lower-dimensional V2 texture responses and limit species-wide claims.
